1 .  These two appeals have been filed being aggrieved by the award dated 20/08/2018 passed by the Second Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Gwalior (M.P.).

sentences.text: The appellants in M.A. No.4379/2018 (Claim Case No.136/2017) are the father and brothers/sister of the deceased- Dharam Singh Chauhan (Gole), while the appellant in M.A. No.1371/2019 (Claim Case No.437/2017) is the widow of the deceased- Dharm Singh Chauhan.
By this common order, both the appeals are being decided in view of involvement of common facts.
Vide impugned award

, learned Claims Tribunal dismissed the claim petition filed by the father and brothers/sister holding that they were not dependent upon the deceased and has awarded Rs.9,88,000/- together with interest only to the widow of the deceased.

2. It is gathered from the records that the proceedings of Claim Case No.437/2017 (filed by widow)
were stayed by the Tribunal under Section 10 of CPC vide order 06/03/2018 and proceedings have been undertaken in Claim Case No.136/2017.
3. The facts which are no more in dispute are that the deceased Dharam Singh was married with non-applicant no.4 on 26/04/2016.

She stayed with the deceased only for a period of four days after Dwarika Prasad Gole vs Dalbeer @ Balveer on 1 April, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19580901/

sentences.text: Dharam Singh met with an accident on 02/06/2016 with a loader vehicle bearing Registration no.MP07- DA-0644 which was owned by non-applicant no.2 and was driven by non- applicant no.1.
The offending vehicle was insured with non-applicant no.3.
It is also not in dispute that Dharam Singh died due to injuries suffered in the accident and non-applicant no.1, 2 & 3 have been held jointly and severely responsible for payment of compensation.
4. Learned Tribunal has dismissed the claim petition filed by the appellants on the ground that they were not dependent upon the deceased Dharam Singh.

It has been held that the appellant no.1, who is the father of the deceased, has failed to substantiate his claim by filing any document to show that he is suffering from diabetes and heart ailment and is unemployed.
It is further held that the appellants have failed to prove that the deceased was giving his salary of Rs.15,000/- to the family for their day to day needs.
Challenging these findings of learned Claims Tribunal, the present appeal has been filed by the appellants.
5. Learned Tribunal has further held that only non-applicant no.4 was dependent upon the deceased and has, thus, awarded whole compensation in her favour.
She has filed M.A. No.1371/2019 seeking enhancement of compensation.
6. For convenience sake, the facts are taken from M.A. No.4379/2018 which is filed by father and brothers/sister of deceased.
The widow is non-applicant no.4 in this appeal.

Regarding dependency of appellants:-
7. Challenging the impugned award, learned counsel for the appellants argued that the appellant no.1, who is the father of the deceased, is suffering from diabetes and heart ailment and was unemployed.
She submitted that entire family was dependent upon the income of the deceased and after his death, the family has rendered without any source of income.
She referred to the statement of appellant no.1 (PW-1) to say that his statement given with regard to his aliment and the income of the deceased has remained unchallenged in the cross- examination.

She further submitted that the evidence with regard to dependency of the family on the income of the deceased is corroborated by the evidence of Amar Singh (PW-4) who is the brother-in-law of the appellant no.1.
8.

Learned counsel further argued that learned Claims Tribunal erred in dismissing the claim petition filed by the appellants solely on the ground that no documentary evidence has been produced to show their dependency upon the deceased.
It is her submission that the appellant no.1 is illiterate and because of his illness, he is not in a position to do even the labour work.
Further, the other appellants were minor at the time of accident and were not supposed to earn.

Learned counsel submitted that learned Claims Tribunal erred in fastening the negative burden upon the appellants instead of shifting the burden upon non- applicants to show that the appellant no.1 was earning.
Regarding non-applicant no.4, learned counsel argued that she stayed with the deceased only for four days after marriage and thereafter, she went to her maternal home.

Immediately thereafter,
deceased met with the accident.
It is her submission that the non- applicant no.4 did not come back to the appellants' house and has entered into re- marriage subsequently.

She, therefore, submitted that the appellants were entitled to get adequate compensation on account of the death of Dharam Dwarika Prasad Gole vs Dalbeer @ Balveer on 1 April, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19580901/
2 Singh.
9.

sentences.text: Refuting the submissions made by appellants' counsel, learned counsel appearing for non-applicant no.4 submitted that admittedly the non-applicant no.4 is the widow of deceased- Dharam Singh.
She is, therefore, entitled to get the compensation.
Further, the appellants have failed to establish that they were dependent upon the income of the deceased.
Rather the deceased was living separately from the family and was not contributing anything towards the survival of the family.
He, thus, submitted that the learned Tribunal is perfectly justified in holding that only non-applicant no.4 was dependent upon the income of the deceased.
Learned counsel further argued that there is no material available on record to show that non-applicant no.4 has entered into re-marriage.
Alternatively he submitted that the dependency has to be assessed on the date of accident and subsequent development would not be a ground for determining the issue.

He, thus,
prayed for dismissal of the appeal filed by the appellants.

10. Considered the arguments and perused the record.
11.
It is not in dispute that appellant no.1 is the father and appellant no.2 to 4 are the brothers/sister of the deceased.
The issue as to whether the appellants were dependent upon the deceased or not, is to be decided based upon the evidence that has come on record.

Notably, learned Claims Tribunal has dismissed the appellants' claim holding that they have failed to bring on record any documentary evidence to show the illness of appellant no.1 and also failed to bring on record any document to show that the deceased was contributing towards survival of the family.
12. Appellant no.1- Dwarika Prasad Gole has been examined as PW-1.

In para 1 & 4 of his statement,
he has specifically stated that he is suffering from diabetes and heart ailment and was dependent upon the income of the deceased.
He has also stated that the deceased was the only earning member of family and after his death, family has rendered without any source of earning.
In para 14, during his cross-examination, he has reiterated the same facts.
In para 17, he has stated that he is illiterate and used to put thumb impression.
In para 26 of his statement the witness has specifically denied that the deceased was living separately and was not taking care of his family.
Reading of his entire statement goes to show that his statement regarding his unemployment and dependency over the income of the deceased, has remained un-rebutted.

13. The aforesaid evidence given by Dwarika Prasad Gole is corroborated with the statement given by Amar Singh (PW-4), who is the brother-in-law (sister's husband), of appellant no.1- Dwarika Prasad Gole.
He is supposed to know about the family affairs of appellants.

In para 3 of his statement, he has supported the stand taken by PW-1.
14.
The fact that the appellant no.1 was earning or not, needs to be decided on the basis of positive evidence.
Non-applicants were required to establish that the appellant no.1 was earning.

However,
learned Tribunal fastened the negative burden upon the appellant to show that he is not earning.
The fact that the appellant no.1 is illiterate and other appellants were minor on the date of accident goes to show that the family was depended upon the income of the deceased.

In her statement,
non-applicant no.4 also could not bring on record any positive evidence to show that appellant no.1 Dwarika Prasad Gole vs Dalbeer @ Balveer on 1 April, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19580901/
3 was earning.

sentences.text: The stand taken by non- applicant no.4 that the deceased was living separately since before the marriage was also not found supported by any evidence.
She also could not refute that she stayed with the deceased only for a period of four days after the marriage.
15. In view of the aforesaid appreciation of evidence, this Court is of the considered view that learned Tribunal erred in holding that appellants were not dependent upon the income of the deceased.
Pertinently, learned Tribunal has not recorded any finding with regard to dependency of appellant no.2 to 4 over the income of the deceased.
It is thus held that the appellants were also dependent upon the income of the deceased while he was earning.

Looking to the peculiar fact of this case that the deceased was married to non-applicant no.4 only 36 days back and she stayed with him only for four days, this Court is of the view that the amount of compensation should be proportionately distributed in the ratio of 55% & 45% each between non-applicant no.4 on one side and the appellants on the other.
This is also because, the appellants are four in number as against non- applicant no.4.

Regarding determination of compensation:-
16.
The other issue to be determined is regarding compensation which is to be awarded to the dependents of the deceased.
The appellants as well as non- applicant no.4 are together on this issue.
Before the Tribunal, they tried to establish that the deceased was earning Rs.15000/- per month as a driver of heavy vehicle owned by one Sanju Chauhan examined as PW-2.
They, however, failed to establish this fact.
Learned Tribunal was justified in holding that the income of the deceased cannot be determined at Rs.15,000/- per month solely based upon the oral testimony of Sanju Chauhan.
The finding of learned Tribunal to this effect is, therefore, upheld.
17. It has come on record that the deceased was a driver of the heavy vehicle who is, thus, required to be accepted as a skilled worker.
As per SALSA guidelines, monthly income of a skilled worker as on the date of accident i.e. 02/06/2016 was Rs.9085/-.
There is no challenge to the finding of Tribunal with regard to age of the deceased which is assessed to be 26 years at the time of accident based upon his license Ex. P/14.
Thus, the multiplier of 17 is rightly applied.
It has come on record that the deceased was married to non-applicant no.4 only 36 days before the accident and she stayed with deceased only for 4 days.
Therefore, in the facts of this case, only for purposes of determining dependency, the deceased has to be treated to be unmarried as he must be spending his income on himself like a bachelor.
The dependency in this case should be taken to be 1/3 instead of half (five dependents including siblings).
Apart from the above, the Tribunal has failed to award any amount towards consortium and future prospects which need to be awarded to the appellants of this appeal.
18. Thus, taking income of the deceased to be Rs.9085/-, his annual income comes to Rs.1,09,020/-.
Adding 40% towards future prospects, the income comes to Rs.1,52,628/-.
Deducting dependency at the rate of 1/3, the annual income of deceased comes to Rs.1,01,752/-.
Applying multiplier of 17, the compensation amount comes to Rs.17,29,784/-.
The dependents are entitled to Rs.15,000/- towards funeral expenses and Rs.15,000/- towards loss of estate, the amount of comes of Rs.17,59,784/-.

The appellants and non-applicant no.4 shall also be entitled to interest at the rate of 6%
per annum from the date of filing of claim petition till actual payment on their respective enhanced amount of compensation.

Regarding court fee to be paid by appellants:-
20.
The issue next to be considered is about the obligation of appellants to pay Ad-valorem court fee on the amount awarded to them by this order.

It be noted that this appeal has been filed by paying court fee of Rs.30/- only while the appeal has been valued at Rs.84,50,000/-.
21.

The learned counsel for appellants referred to provisions of Article 11(a)
(i) of Court Fees Act, 1870, as amended for the State of Madhya Pradesh, and submitted that the said provision casts an obligation to pay Ad-valorem court fee on a claimant only when the appeal is presented seeking enhancement of compensation as awarded by claims tribunal.
As per her submission, the Ad- valorem court fee is not payable when the claim petition has been dismissed and no compensation is awarded by claims tribunal.
In support of her submission, the learned counsel relied upon order passed in the case of R.P. Gupta vs. State of M.P. in R.P. No.124/2012.

sentences.text: She thus submitted that since the claim petition of appellants has been dismissed by tribunal, they are not liable to pay Ad-valorem court fee on the appeal.
22. On the other hand, the learned counsel appearing for non-applicants refuted the submissions made by counsel for appellants.

They submitted that the appellants are being awarded compensation by this court which amounts to enhancement of compensation from 'zero' and they are liable to pay the Ad- valorem court fee on the amount awarded to them by this court in this appeal.

23. Considered the arguments of learned counsel for respective parties.
24.

Under Article 11(a)(i) of Schedule II of Court Fees Act, 1870, as amended by M.P. Act No.6 of 2008 and further by M.P. Act No.3 of 2013, in an appeal filed against an award passed by the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, the claimant is required to pay Ad-valorem court Fee at the prescribed rate, which at present is 2.5%, for enhancement of amount of award passed by Tribunal.
In other words, the court fee is payable on the difference between the amount of compensation awarded by Tribunal and the amount claimed in the appeal.

The relevant extract of the Court Fee Act, 1870, as amended by Act No.6 of 2008 and by Act No.3 of 2013 reads as under:

25. The use of the term 'for enhancement of amount of award passed by Motor Accident Claims Tribunal' would necessarily mean the difference of amount of compensation awarded by Tribunal and the one claimed in appeal before the High Court.
In other words, the ad-valorem court fee is payable by claimants on the difference of amount of compensation awarded by Tribunal and the one claimed in appeal before the High Court.
26. There can be two contingencies that may arise in appeal under Section 173 of MV Act before High Court in cases where the claim petition has been dismissed by Tribunal.
There may be cases where the appeal is allowed by High Court and while setting aside the award of Tribunal, the matter needs to be remitted to Tribunal for determination of compensation.
In such cases, there is no enhancement of compensation by High Court and therefore, claimant is not required to pay ad-valorem court fee.

However, there can be cases where, after setting aside the award of Tribunal,
the High Court also determines the amount of compensation, as has been done in this case.
In such cases, there is enhancement of compensation from 'zero' to the amount determined by High Court in appeal.
In such cases, the claimants are required to pay the Ad-valorem court fee.
27. Another issue that crop up for consideration is as to how the claimants would value their appeal as their claim petition has been dismissed by Tribunal?
The answer to this issue is simple.
As the claimants value their appeal in case of enhancement of compensation, they should value their appeal also in case of dismissal of their claim petition.
If they are of opinion that determination of compensation is not possible in appeal for want of necessary evidence regarding income etc., they may value their appeal and pay fix court fee.

However, if there is sufficient material available on record to determine compensation in appeal itself and there is no need to remand the matter, in that case, they should value the appeal accordingly and pay Ad-valorem court fee in appeal.
28. Thus, in view of discussion made above, the appellants are required to pay the Ad-valorem court fee in their appeal.
They have, however, valued their appeal on Rs.84.50 lakh.
